public_rationale: The claim has two parts. The first part holds. In 2023, Crunchbase described AI as the standout force in venture funding: an 'AI fervor' without which totals 'would have been even lower', and AI's share of funding was rising (e1, e2). The second part, 'very little else', does not hold on the data. AI was about 18% of global venture funding in H1 2023, and more than half of that was one OpenAI round, so most money went elsewhere (e2). Large non-AI rounds closed in Q2 (e4). In July 2023, the last month reported before the post, AI took about 11% of funding. Health care, renewable energy and financial services each raised more than AI (e3). Crunchbase said AI 'did not stand out' that month. Venture was clearly excited about AI, but it kept funding other sectors at larger totals. 'Very little else' overstates this.
limitations: 'Enamored' and 'very little else' are rhetorical; the result depends on reading them through funding data.
Funding totals measure where money went, not VC attention or hype, which may have been more lopsided toward AI.
Crunchbase sector labels can overlap, and data for recent months is revised upward over time.
The full-year 2023 US figure (AI about one-third of dollars) is later and broader than the claim period, so it is context only.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: As of August 2023, venture capital is focused on AI and little else, despite there being plenty of revenue-generating companies with good ideas to invest in.

statement.excerpt: There are plenty of companies to invest in, companies that have good ideas that generate revenues, but venture is still enamored with AI and very little else.

from_speaker: "plenty of companies to invest in, companies that have good ideas that generate revenues"
present tense, post dated 2023-08-10; "still" points to a state that had lasted for some time
our_interpretation: The claim has two parts. Part A: AI was the main focus of venture enthusiasm in mid-2023. Part B: venture showed 'very little' interest in anything else.

He gave no measure. Plain reading: where venture money and attention went in 2023 up to the post. AI counts as the focus if data and reporting single it out as the standout or 'bright spot' sector. 'Very little else' counts as true if non-AI sectors drew only a small part of venture money or interest. It counts as false if most venture money still went to non-AI sectors, or if other sectors drew …

Because of 'still', the period runs from the start of 2023 (after ChatGPT's launch) to the post date. This covers both the Q2 AI surge and the latest monthly data before the post (July 2023). It is not limited to one month.
'Very little else' is read as strong but ordinary wording. It is not read as literally zero, and it is not read as just a figure of speech that means nothing.
The clause about 'plenty of companies ... that generate revenues' is framing and opinion about investable firms. It is not scored separately.
Weak non-AI funding fits his wider point that VCs were hoarding cash. The test is whether AI was the overriding focus of the money that was invested, not whether total investment was low.
criteria.support_condition: Data from 2023 up to the post shows AI as the clear standout in venture investment, and non-AI sectors drawing only a small part of venture money or interest.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Data from the same period shows that most venture money still went to non-AI sectors, or that other single sectors outdrew AI, so that 'very little else' does not hold. Strong AI enthusiasm alone would not contradict Part A.

evidence.excerpt: It’s safe to say that without the AI fervor kicked off by the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in November, venture funding so far in 2023 would have been even lower.
evidence.explanation: Supports Part A. Crunchbase singles out AI 'fervor' as the standout force in H1 2023 venture funding while overall funding fell.

evidence.excerpt: Companies categorized as AI in Crunchbase raised $25 billion in the first half of 2023, representing 18% of global funding.
evidence.explanation: AI's share was rising, but it was 18% of H1 2023 global funding, and over half of that was one OpenAI round. About 82% went to non-AI companies, which is hard to square with 'very little else'.

evidence.excerpt: Funding to AI companies was around $2 billion — about 11% of all venture funding — in July. Health care and biotech companies raised around $3.8 billion, renewable energy around $3.1 billion, and financial services companies raised $2.9 billion this past month.
evidence.explanation: In the last full month before the post, three non-AI sectors each raised more venture money than AI. The same section says AI 'did not stand out as a sector'. This cuts against 'very little else'.

evidence.excerpt: Companies in sectors outside of AI also raised large rounds, including China-based fast fashion retailer Shein, Germany-based solar and smart electricity company 1Komma5°, and Sweden-based battery manufacturer Northvolt.
evidence.explanation: Shows large Q2 2023 venture rounds outside AI, in retail, solar and batteries.

evidence.excerpt: AI startups attracted one out of every three dollars invested in the U.S. last year, reflecting a surge in investor interest after OpenAI’s ChatGPT grabbed the spotlight
evidence.publisher: The Globe and Mail (Reuters, citing PitchBook)
evidence.explanation: Full-year 2023 US data shows a strong surge in AI interest, but a third of dollars is still well short of 'very little else'. It is context only because it covers all of 2023, past the post date, and the US only.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A measure of VC attention, such as the share of new deals, term sheets or partner time going to AI versus other sectors in mid-2023, showing AI crowding out nearly everything else, would support the 'very little else' part. Current funding data contradicts it.
